classification_signals: Introduction describes it as a literature review prepared in relation to a networking event (WUF9) and drawing upon existing bodies of studies (Page 1)

The paper synthesizes information from various cited sources to discuss issues related to semi-public spaces for different groups (e.g., children, migrants, elderly, disabled, women) and themes (consumption, economy).
Extensive bibliography (Pages 15-17) supports the review nature.
title: LITERATURE REVIEW ON SEMI-PUBLIC SPACE AND THE NEW URBAN AGENDA: STAKEHOLDERS AND ISSUES

findings.consequent: Increased liveability, health, mobility, navigation options in cities
findings.quote: if urban public spaces were to be more accessible particularly to the ageing population and those with different experiential habits, cities, cities would be more liveable and healthier, with better mobility and navigation options.

findings.antecedent: Public spaces with good access to facilities (shops, cafés)
findings.consequent: Increased social involvement amongst older people
findings.quote: research has found that, where there are public spaces with good access to facilities like shops and cafés, there are higher levels of social involvement amongst older people.

findings.antecedent: Production and consumption of meta-public spaces (digital augmentation)
findings.consequent: Blurring of private/public distinction; transformation of public space into 'pseudospace of interaction'
findings.quote: In the production and consumption of meta-public spaces in today's cities in the face of globalised spaces of flows, the distinction between private and public becomes blurred, whereby public space is transformed into a 'pseudospace of interaction' (Manfredini, 2017b, p. 428).

findings.antecedent: Communication-based digital augmented public spaces
findings.consequent: Increased re-politicisation, individual empowerment, de-privatisation
findings.quote: Communication-based digital augmented public spaces may support the re-politicisation, empowering individuals and de-privatisation.

findings.antecedent: Tourism and global flows
findings.consequent: Commodification of cultural elements; staging of culture; transformation of urban spaces into spectacles; loss of authenticity
findings.quote: In the space of tourism and, indeed, today's space of flows, cultural elements which are embedded in places, spaces, and communities, become commodified. Culture is staged and the original context is disconnected from its specific socio-cultural references. Urban spaces are transformed, decontextualised and distorted into venues for exotic spectacles. As Robert Shepherd (2002) claims, “what was once pure and authentic has become spoiled and commodified” (p. 183).

findings.antecedent: Informal income-generating processes in public spaces (e.g., street vendors)
findings.consequent: Increased threats (theft, illness, police raids, over-regulation); reduced voice in policy-making
findings.quote: Those working in the informal economy in public spaces are also prone to theft, illness, as well as police raids and seizures. In the case of Bogotá, Colombia, such vendors have little voice in policy-making in their interface with local politicians in addressing their issues (Donovan, 2008).

findings.antecedent: Encouragement of entrepreneurship and informal economic activities (via public space appropriation/adaptation)
findings.consequent: Increased businesses, vibrancy, social interaction
findings.quote: From the discussions at the WUF, cities needed to encourage entrepreneurship and other informal economic activities through appropriation and adaptation of public spaces, such that people can create businesses and vibrancy, as well as promote social interaction between inhabitants.

findings.antecedent: Increasing blur of public/private realms (technology, hyper-consumerism); augmented spatialities (digital spheres)
findings.consequent: Main access to public sphere; re-politicisation; individual empowerment; new meta-public space
findings.quote: In the wake of the increasing blur of public and private realms in today's cities, brought about by technological advancements and the inherent contradictions of hyper-consumerism, augmented spatialities mediated through communication-based digital spheres provide the main access to the public sphere in public spaces, constituting a form of re-politicisation and empowerment of the individual in a new form of open, permeable, and recombinant meta-public space.

findings.antecedent: Attention to opportunities/limitations of blurred spatiality; recognition of diverse locales/actors
findings.consequent: Public spaces working well for everyone; exercise of right to the city/citizenship in democratic, participative, pluralist urban space production
findings.quote: Recommendations were made to pay particular attention to the opportunities and limitations of the global spread of the new complex blurred spatiality whilst simultaneously recognising the differences of the diverse locale and range of actors and their issues in urban public spaces. This can guarantee the exercise of the right to the city and citizenship in a democratic, participative, and pluralist production of the urban space.

limitations: The New Urban Agenda (NUA) overlooks culture and consumption (Page 2).
Findings from the WUF9 event are qualitative themes derived from discussions of 'more than 40 participants' and group summaries, not rigorous statistical analyses (Page 2).
minimum_safe_summary: This literature review synthesizes findings from a UN-Habitat networking event (WUF9) and existing studies to explore semi-public space issues within the New Urban Agenda (NUA). It identifies socio-spatial problems and opportunities for various stakeholders, including children, youth, elderly, differently-abled, indigenous people, marginalized genders, and migrants, across themes of social integration, consumption, and economy. Key findings highlight how urban environments impact children's play and well-being, how migrants appropriate public spaces, and how design influences safety and accessibility for diverse groups. The paper also discusses the blurring of public and private realms due to digital augmentation, leading to 'meta-public spaces' and the commodification of culture in tourism. It notes that informal economic activities in public spaces face significant threats. A key limitation is that the NUA overlooks culture and consumption, and the WUF9 event's findings are qualitative themes from discussions rather than statistical analyses.

mechanism_chain.description: Spatial segregation, often manifested through design, ownership, or access policies of semi-public spaces, limits opportunities for diverse social interaction and resource sharing, thereby reinforcing social divisions and leading to social and economic exclusion for marginalized groups.
